cells.tense: Right now the plan in front of you and the evenness of it are both being held.
cells.act: notice what you already know before you reason about it
cells.ask: Before the next planning pass, put your first take on the priority at the top of the list and fit the rest around it.
cells.core:
What you're running is fair on its face. Jobs get done, credit lands where it's earned, and nothing piles up uneven behind the scenes. The schedule has weight but it isn't punishing anyone. You aren't forcing the pieces together here; you've found the shape they want.

Underneath that, your read on what matters keeps landing clean, and it's worth using first. Before the next planning pass, take your first take on the priority and set it at the top — then fit the rest around it instead of deciding late and checking after. If that first take turns out wrong, the plan still has a spine, and you've lost an hour, not a week.

cells.verb: Turn scattered pieces into a shape that holds.

cells.tense: You're planning for a version of this that hasn't arrived yet, and the rails are going up in advance.
cells.act: step back far enough to see the whole arrangement
cells.ask: Look at how the whole arrangement fits together — the layout, apart from this week's worry — before you add another piece.
cells.core:
You've built the fence before the field. The plan has columns for things that may not happen, contingencies for people who haven't spoken, and the structure has stopped following the work and started leading it. From outside it looks like control; from inside it feels like care.

The correction is distance, not effort. Look at how the whole thing fits together — the shape of it apart from this one hard week — and see which parts you invented. The arrangement is likely simpler than the version in your head. Nothing has to come down yet; just get far enough from it that you can see all of it at once.

cells.tense: You've been standing at a doorway for a while, and the room past it has already changed.
cells.act: let one structure collapse that could not hold
cells.ask: Find something you've been propping up that can't hold, and keep your hands off it for a few days.
cells.core:
The pieces stay separate. Try to sequence them and the order won't stick, and you end up shuffling the same stack of half-starts. It isn't a failure of effort — the frame you keep reaching for is the wrong size, or made for another room. If the ground beneath you feels clear and empty, that's what being between forms feels like.

Breakthrough here isn't a big bang. Find something you've been propping up — a habit, a plan, a hold — and keep your hands off it this week. Stop carrying it. The ground clears by itself once something false goes down. If nothing falls, you've learned what you were holding, which is worth having.

cells.tense: The room is already arranged, and it arranged itself while you were looking elsewhere.
cells.act: mark the end of it with a plain act
cells.ask: When something you quietly sorted out is finished today, mark it done with one plain act — close it, write the line, switch off the lamp.
cells.core:
Something you do regularly keeps the place standing. People find what they need because you moved it; decisions get made because you laid out the order when nobody was watching. You put it down to instinct, or just getting by. It isn't that. You're holding up a structure and not claiming it.

Cleanup isn't what's needed here; a record is. When the next thing you quietly organize is finished, mark it done with one plain act — close the folder, write the line, switch off the lamp. That's your name on it. The structure stays useful, and you stop being the one whose orders go unsigned.
